facts.fact_text: The applicants opposed reforms initiated by the new Tbilisi State University administration as part of the nation-wide higher education reform in 2004-2005.
The applicants held numerous public meetings at Tbilisi State University as part of their activities opposing the reforms.
The applicants made public statements denouncing what they called the 'destruction' of Tbilisi State University.
The applicants wrote to various public officials denouncing what they called the 'destruction' of Tbilisi State University.
The Grand Academic Council led the protests against the changes at Tbilisi State University.
On 19 June 2006 the already-dissolved Grand Academic Council organised a meeting of Tbilisi State University staff.

After the meeting with Mr G.Kh. ended without results, Tbilisi State University employees — including all of the applicants — decided to stay at the University in one of the lecture halls and hold a further meeting among themselves.
On 20 June 2006 the applicants, along with other employees of Tbilisi State University, gathered again in one of the lecture halls of the University.

On 3 July 2006, in response to a request by the fourth applicant, Mr Sanadze, the acting Rector of Tbilisi State University, Mr G.Kh., authorised a meeting of University employees in the Grand Hall of the main University building between 3.30 p.m. and 7 p.m.
At the meeting of 3 July 2006, the already-dissolved Grand Academic Council 'elected' the second applicant as the new Rector of Tbilisi State University.

After the 'election' of the second applicant as new Rector, a group of about twenty people, including all of the applicants, headed to the office of acting Rector Mr G.Kh. to inform him of the Grand Academic Council's decision and to demand his resignation.

According to the case file, after their removal from the acting Rector's office, the applicants together with other protesters — totalling approximately 400 people — gathered in one of the lecture halls of the main Tbilisi State University building and continued their protest.

At the 3 August 2006 hearing, the applicants' lawyers argued that the applicants had simply been exercising their right to freedom of assembly and freedom of expression as provided for in the Constitution of Georgia.

In their appeal, the applicants challenged the categorisation of their actions as administrative offences by the Tbilisi City Court, submitting that they had simply been exercising their freedom of expression and freedom of assembly.
Article 24(1) of the Constitution of Georgia provides that everyone shall be free to receive and impart information, to express and disseminate his or her opinion orally, in writing, or otherwise.

Article 25(1) of the Constitution of Georgia provides that everyone, except those serving in the military forces and the Ministry of Internal Affairs, shall have the right to gather publicly, unarmed, both indoors and outdoors, without prior permission.

Article 1(1) of the Law of Georgia on Assembly and Demonstrations, as worded at the material time, provided that the law regulates the exercise of the right guaranteed by the Constitution of Georgia to gather publicly, unarmed, both indoors and outdoors, without prior permission.
According to the applicants, at around 1 a.m. on 20 June 2006 the police arrived at Tbilisi State University.
According to the applicants, the police forced everyone out of the Tbilisi State University building without giving any explanations or prior warning.
According to the applicants, despite the applicants' repeated requests, the police officers did not show them any order authorising the removal of the people gathered at Tbilisi State University.
Towards the evening of 20 June 2006 the police allegedly again dispersed the applicants' meeting at Tbilisi State University.
While the meeting at acting Rector Mr G.Kh.'s office continued, the police entered the Tbilisi State University grounds.
The police officers went directly to the office of acting Rector Mr G.Kh., who immediately left the room upon their arrival.
According to the applicants, after the police asked the applicants and others present to leave the acting Rector's office, they left without any resistance and moved to a lecture hall.
The applicants alleged that at around 11 p.m. on 3 July 2006 the police closed the doors of the lecture hall and prevented the people inside from leaving.
The applicants alleged that they had been locked in the lecture hall without access to water, food or toilet facilities until approximately 8-10 a.m. on 4 July 2006.

On 3 July 2006 criminal proceedings were initiated under Article 226 of the Criminal Code of Georgia against unidentified perpetrators in respect of the organisation and participation in group actions violating public order.

On 5 July 2006 the second, fourth, fifth, seventh and eighth applicants were questioned as witnesses in the course of the criminal proceedings initiated on 3 July 2006 under Article 226 of the Criminal Code of Georgia.
On 29 July 2006 the relevant prosecutor issued a ruling terminating the criminal proceedings concerning the alleged organisation and participation in group actions violating public order.

The prosecutor's ruling of 29 July 2006 stated that the applicants had committed administrative offences — namely arbitrary behaviour under Article 174 of the Code of Administrative Offences, a minor violation of public order under Article 166 of the Code of Administrative Offences, and disobeying the lawful instructions of law-enforcement personnel under Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

In the operative part of the prosecutor's ruling of 29 July 2006, the prosecutor stated that the ruling, along with the case file, was to be sent to the Tbilisi City Court in order for administrative proceedings to be conducted against the applicants.
At the same time as being served with the ruling, the applicants were told that a hearing in the administrative proceedings initiated against them had been scheduled for the next day, 30 July 2006.
On 30 July 2006 a hearing took place at the Tbilisi City Court in the administrative proceedings against the applicants.

By a decision of 4 August 2006, the Tbilisi City Court found the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, seventh and eighth applicants guilty of administrative offences under Articles 166, 173 and 174 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The Tbilisi City Court imposed a fine of 100 Georgian laris (approximately 45 euros) on each of the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, seventh and eighth applicants.

The Tbilisi City Court terminated the proceedings concerning the alleged disobeying of a lawful order given by the police under Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences with respect to the sixth applicant, Ms Sikharulidze, and the ninth applicant, Mr D. Bakhtadze, finding that they had left the acting Rector's office before the arrival of the police.

The Tbilisi City Court found the sixth applicant, Ms Sikharulidze, and the ninth applicant, Mr D. Bakhtadze, guilty of administrative offences under Articles 166 and 174 of the Code of Administrative Offences only, imposing a fine of 100 Georgian laris on each of them.
On 4 September 2006, the chairwoman of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal, sitting privately and without holding an oral hearing, dismissed the applicants' appeal as unsubstantiated.

In the letter authorising the gathering on 3 July 2006, acting Rector Mr G.Kh. stressed that participants were asked to maintain order and to conclude the meeting before 7 p.m.

Article 25(3) of the Constitution of Georgia provides that authorities may terminate a public assembly or a manifestation only if it assumes an unlawful character.

Article 9(1) of the Law of Georgia on Assembly and Demonstrations, as worded at the material time, prohibited holding an assembly or a demonstration inside the building of the Parliament of Georgia, the residency of the President of Georgia, the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court of Georgia, on the premises of courts, prosecutor's offices or of police, penitentiary or military units and sites, in railway stations, airports, hospitals or diplomatic missions (or within a 20-metre radius thereof), on the premises of governmental institutions or local self-government bodies, or in the buildings of companies, institutions and organisations that operate under special labour security rules or are under armed guard.

Under Article 9 of the Law on the Police, as in force at the material time, the police were responsible inter alia for dispersing unlawful rallies, demonstrations, pickets and other assemblies that posed a threat to public safety, the lives and health of people, property, and other rights guaranteed by law.

Article 166 of the Code of Administrative Offences of Georgia, as in force at the material time, defined minor hooliganism (a minor breach of public order) as swearing and cursing in a public place, causing insulting harassment to a person, or other similar actions which disturb public order and peace, punishable by a fine of 100 Georgian laris or, if that measure was not deemed sufficient, up to thirty days' administrative detention.

Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences of Georgia, as in force at the material time, provided that maliciously disobeying a lawful instruction or order issued by a law enforcement officer shall be punishable by a fine amounting to ten times the minimum monthly wage, or by one to six months' correctional labour compounded by the withholding of 20% of the offender's wages, or, if those measures were not deemed sufficient, by up to thirty days' administrative detention.

Article 174 of the Code of Administrative Offences of Georgia, as in force at the material time, defined arbitrary behaviour as the exercise of a right in violation of a law which does not cause any significant damage to people, the State or to public bodies, punishable by a warning or a fine of half the minimum monthly wage, or in the case of public officials, a warning or a fine of one minimum monthly wage.
In the letter authorising the gathering on 3 July 2006, acting Rector Mr G.Kh. stressed that participants were asked to maintain order and to conclude the meeting before 7 p.m.

According to the Government's official version of events, the Tbilisi State University security service was no longer in control of the situation and the functioning of the University administration was disrupted.
According to the Government's official version of events, the police were called to restore order because the applicants and other protesters were refusing to leave.

The Tbilisi State University staff members who were eyewitnesses claimed that the University had remained paralysed during the incident, with several meetings being disrupted and acting Rector Mr G.Kh. and several members of the University administration being prevented from carrying out their duties.

Acting Rector Mr G.Kh. testified that the incident in his office had lasted for about an hour and a half, paralysing not only his work but the functioning of the whole administration of Tbilisi State University.

At the hearing of 3 August 2006, V.J. stated that various protesters had been making insulting statements and noise and that as a result the work in the main building of Tbilisi State University had been disrupted.

In connection with the charge of a minor breach of public order (minor hooliganism), the Tbilisi City Court established that the applicants had burst into the office of acting Rector Mr G.Kh., calling for his resignation.
The Tbilisi City Court established that the applicants had demanded, in an insulting manner, that acting Rector Mr G.Kh. immediately leave his office and take all his belongings with him.

The Tbilisi City Court concluded that the applicants had occupied the office of acting Rector Mr G.Kh. against his will for about two hours and had disregarded his repeated requests for them to leave.

The Tbilisi City Court concluded that the applicants' behaviour had amounted to insulting harassment with respect to Mr G.Kh. and other staff present, and to 'other similar action' that had violated public order and peace.

The Tbilisi City Court concluded that although persons are entitled to exercise the rights and freedoms enshrined in Articles 19, 24 and 25 of the Constitution of Georgia, they are obliged in the process of exercising those rights to abstain from violating others' rights and interests, from encroaching upon others' honour and dignity, and from violating public order.
The Tbilisi City Court established that the remaining applicants had refused to leave the office of acting Rector Mr G.Kh. despite the repeated requests of the police.

The Tbilisi City Court concluded that the applicants' refusal for more than an hour to obey the orders of the police, notwithstanding the fact that no physical force had been used, had amounted to a breach of Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

Article 24(4) of the Constitution of Georgia provides that the exercise of the rights listed in Article 24(1) and (2) may be subject only to such limitations as are prescribed by law and are necessary in a democratic society in the interests of state security, territorial integrity or public safety, to prevent crime, to safeguard rights and dignity of others, to prevent disclosure of information acknowledged as confidential, or to ensure the independence and impartiality of justice.

According to the applicants, they asked Mr G.Kh. to leave his office, but he refused to do so.

According to the Government's official version of events, it took more than one hour for the police to negotiate the applicants' removal from the acting Rector's office.

The Tbilisi State University staff members who were eyewitnesses to the events of 3 July 2006 all identified the applicants as being among those who had forced their way into acting Rector Mr G.Kh.'s office, insulted him and demanded his resignation.

The Tbilisi State University staff members who were eyewitnesses noted that while there had been no physical confrontation, the group of 'protesting professors' had been acting in a highly disrespectful manner, chanting insulting expressions against Mr G.Kh.

Acting Rector Mr G.Kh. testified that their meeting had continued against a background of noise and chanting, with protesters chanting 'leave, leave'.

Acting Rector Mr G.Kh. testified that he had not been personally insulted, although his colleagues had told him that protesters in the corridor adjacent to his office had been chanting insulting slogans.
In reply to a direct question, acting Rector Mr G.Kh. explained that no foul language had been used by protesters in his office, either in respect of him or of his colleagues.

Acting Rector Mr G.Kh. testified that the incident in his office had lasted for about an hour and a half, paralysing not only his work but the functioning of the whole administration of Tbilisi State University.

The Tbilisi State University security service members confirmed that a large group of about fifty people, in disobedience of orders given by the security service, had entered the reception area of the acting Rector's office by force.

The Tbilisi State University security service members confirmed that around fifteen or twenty people had forced their way into acting Rector Mr G.Kh.'s office, where they stayed for about two hours until the police secured their removal.
The prosecutor concluded in the ruling of 29 July 2006 that the actions of the applicants had not comprised elements of a crime.

The prosecutor's ruling of 29 July 2006 stated that the applicants had committed administrative offences — namely arbitrary behaviour under Article 174 of the Code of Administrative Offences, a minor violation of public order under Article 166 of the Code of Administrative Offences, and disobeying the lawful instructions of law-enforcement personnel under Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
At the hearing of 30 July 2006, the applicants complained that they had not had sufficient time to acquaint themselves with the relevant material in the case file and to hire a lawyer.
At the hearing of 30 July 2006, the applicants requested that acting Rector Mr G.Kh. and the security staff of Tbilisi State University be questioned.
At the hearing on 3 August 2006, the applicants reiterated their request for acting Rector Mr G.Kh. to be examined in court.

At the hearing on 3 August 2006, the applicants requested that the court hear the deputy Rector of Tbilisi State University and four other eyewitnesses to the events of 3 July 2006, including two journalists who had not been questioned at the pre-trial stage of the discontinued criminal proceedings.

At the hearing on 3 August 2006, the judge refused the applicants' request for the questioning of acting Rector Mr G.Kh. and his deputy, reasoning that those two individuals had already been questioned at the pre-trial stage and that their statements had been included in the case file.

According to the minutes of the 3 August 2006 hearing, the applicants challenged the factual circumstances of the events of 3 July 2006 as presented by the prosecutor, maintaining that they had not broken into the acting Rector's office but had entered it and sat there calmly without using any force.

According to the minutes of the 3 August 2006 hearing, the applicants maintained that they had not insulted or threatened acting Rector Mr G.Kh. but had simply presented him with the decision of the Grand Academic Council.

According to the minutes of the 3 August 2006 hearing, the applicants maintained that they had not disobeyed the instructions of the police but had left the acting Rector's office within ten or fifteen minutes of being ordered to do so by the police.
At the 3 August 2006 hearing, the applicants' lawyers argued that the acting Rector's office did not constitute a public space for the purposes of Article 166 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

At the 3 August 2006 hearing, the applicants' lawyers argued that the applicants had simply been exercising their right to freedom of assembly and freedom of expression as provided for in the Constitution of Georgia.

At the 3 August 2006 hearing, the applicants reiterated their complaint that they had been locked in the Tbilisi State University lecture hall for the night of 3-4 July 2006 without access to water or toilets.

At the 3 August 2006 hearing, the applicants tried to put several questions to the prosecutor regarding the alleged locking in the lecture hall, but the presiding judge dismissed the questions as irrelevant and having no bearing on the case.

At the hearing of 3 August 2006, police patrol officer G.Ch. clarified in reply to a question that no one had physically resisted the police, but that the protesters had simply refused to leave the acting Rector's office.
At the hearing of 3 August 2006, police patrol officer G.Ch. specified that insulting statements had been made by protesters in the corridor and not in the acting Rector's office.

At the hearing of 3 August 2006, police officer Z.S. confirmed that while no force had been used, the police had spent an hour persuading a group of about twenty people to leave the acting Rector's office.

At the hearing of 3 August 2006, the third police officer, K.B., similarly maintained that there had been no physical confrontation inside the acting Rector's office, but that it had taken a while before those inside had agreed to leave.

The two journalists and two professors questioned on 3 August 2006 all claimed that there had been no confrontation — either physical or verbal — in the office of acting Rector Mr G.Kh. on 3 July 2006.

The two journalists and two professors questioned on 3 August 2006 claimed that the group had been simply demanding the resignation of Mr G.Kh. and that they had left the office at the request of the police.

The Tbilisi City Court imposed a fine of 100 Georgian laris (approximately 45 euros) on each of the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, seventh and eighth applicants.

Bakhtadze, finding that they had left the acting Rector's office before the arrival of the police.

The Tbilisi City Court found the sixth applicant, Ms Sikharulidze, and the ninth applicant, Mr D. Bakhtadze, guilty of administrative offences under Articles 166 and 174 of the Code of Administrative Offences only, imposing a fine of 100 Georgian laris on each of them.

The Tbilisi City Court found that the subsequent demand for the resignation of acting Rector Mr G.Kh. in view of the election had been unlawful and constituted the administrative offence of arbitrary behaviour within the meaning of Article 174 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

In connection with the charge of a minor breach of public order (minor hooliganism), the Tbilisi City Court established that the applicants had burst into the office of acting Rector Mr G.Kh., calling for his resignation.
The Tbilisi City Court established that the applicants had demanded, in an insulting manner, that acting Rector Mr G.Kh. immediately leave his office and take all his belongings with him.

The Tbilisi City Court concluded that the applicants had occupied the office of acting Rector Mr G.Kh. against his will for about two hours and had disregarded his repeated requests for them to leave.

The Tbilisi City Court concluded that the applicants' behaviour had amounted to insulting harassment with respect to Mr G.Kh. and other staff present, and to 'other similar action' that had violated public order and peace.

The Tbilisi City Court dismissed the applicants' argument that the acting Rector's office was merely a private working space, reasoning that the presence of the public rendered it a public space for the purposes of the Code of Administrative Offences.

The Tbilisi City Court concluded that although persons are entitled to exercise the rights and freedoms enshrined in Articles 19, 24 and 25 of the Constitution of Georgia, they are obliged in the process of exercising those rights to abstain from violating others' rights and interests, from encroaching upon others' honour and dignity, and from violating public order.
The Tbilisi City Court concluded that the applicants had, in exercising their constitutional rights, committed acts prohibited by law on 3 July 2006 in the office of the acting Rector.

The Tbilisi City Court concluded that the sixth applicant, Ms Sikharulidze, and the ninth applicant, Mr D. Bakhtadze, had left the office of acting Rector Mr G.Kh. before the arrival of the police and were thus acquitted of the charge of disobeying a lawful order given by the police under Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The Tbilisi City Court established that the remaining applicants had refused to leave the office of acting Rector Mr G.Kh. despite the repeated requests of the police.

The Tbilisi City Court concluded that the applicants' refusal for more than an hour to obey the orders of the police, notwithstanding the fact that no physical force had been used, had amounted to a breach of Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences.

In their appeal, the applicants complained that there had been no record of an administrative offence having been made individually in respect of each of them and that their individual roles in the commission of the impugned administrative offences had not been established.
In their appeal, the applicants complained that the proceedings had been brought in a manner suggesting their collective liability.

In their appeal, the applicants referred to witness statements noting that there had been two hundred people outside and twenty people inside the acting Rector's office during the events of 3 July 2006 and that it was impossible to identify the individuals who had allegedly insulted the acting Rector and forced their way into his office.
In their appeal, the applicants complained of the failure of the Tbilisi City Court to examine acting Rector Mr G.Kh. and his deputy in the course of the trial.

In their appeal, the applicants challenged the categorisation of their actions as administrative offences by the Tbilisi City Court, submitting that they had simply been exercising their freedom of expression and freedom of assembly.
On 4 September 2006, the chairwoman of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal, sitting privately and without holding an oral hearing, dismissed the applicants' appeal as unsubstantiated.
The chairwoman of the Tbilisi Court of Appeal concluded that the decision of the Tbilisi City Court had been lawful and properly reasoned.

As shown in Imedi's recording of the events of 3 July 2006, some of those who entered the reception area had walked into the acting Rector's office itself, notifying Mr G.Kh. of the decision of the Grand Academic Council and demanding his resignation.

On 24 July 2006 several members of the former Grand Academic Council, including the second, third, fourth, fifth and seventh applicants, sent a letter to the President of Georgia complaining about the events of 19-20 June and 3-4 July 2006.

In the letter of 24 July 2006 to the President of Georgia, the applicants made a particular complaint that they, along with several hundred other people, had been locked in the Tbilisi State University lecture hall for the whole night of 3-4 July 2006.

In the letter of 24 July 2006 to the President of Georgia, the applicants alleged that being locked in the lecture hall had amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment, as they had been denied access to drinking water and a toilet and had been left without fresh air.
In the letter of 24 July 2006 to the President of Georgia, the applicants requested the initiation of criminal proceedings regarding the events of 3-4 July 2006.
A copy of the letter of 24 July 2006 was sent to the Prosecutor General of Georgia.
In support of their request, the applicants submitted statements given by fifteen people accounting in detail for the events of 19-20 June and 3-4 July 2006.

In the ruling of 29 July 2006, the prosecutor also decided to terminate proceedings that had apparently been opened against police officers in respect of their alleged unlawful use of force on 3-4 July 2006, finding the complaint lodged by the applicants in that connection unsubstantiated.
The prosecutor's ruling of 29 July 2006 did not mention the applicants' complaint concerning the events of 19-20 June 2006.

At the 3 August 2006 hearing, the applicants reiterated their complaint that they had been locked in the Tbilisi State University lecture hall for the night of 3-4 July 2006 without access to water or toilets.

At the 3 August 2006 hearing, the applicants tried to put several questions to the prosecutor regarding the alleged locking in the lecture hall, but the presiding judge dismissed the questions as irrelevant and having no bearing on the case.
